title: Team and operations
summary: How to grow from one buyer into a team that runs without you in every chat: hiring and training buyers, spending authority, SOPs, a lean tools stack, reporting that drives decisions and a steady creative pipeline. It closes with written pay plans that reward confirmed profit inside the rules, so the team scales the business you want.

lessons.title: Hiring media buyers
objectives: By the end you can write a scorecard for the buyer you actually need.
By the end you can run a paid test task and a trial period that show real ability.
By the end you can estimate what a new buyer costs and how long they take to pay back.

steps.h: Hire when the work is proven
steps.p: Hire a buyer to run more of something that already works, not to find something that works for you. A new person cannot be judged fairly on a problem you have not solved yourself, and you will not know what good looks like.

d.b: Hire to scale a system, not to find one
d.s: Prove it yourself first, then teach it

steps.say: Here's the first rule of hiring. Hire a buyer to run more of something that already works, not to find something that works for you. Why? If you haven't solved the problem yourself, you can't judge a new person fairly, and you won't even know what good looks like. So prove it yourself first, then teach it. Hire to scale a system, not to find one.

steps.h: Signs you are ready to hire
steps.p: Hiring too early burns cash and morale. Hiring too late burns you out and leaves winning campaigns unwatched. These signs suggest the timing is right.
d: You have at least one stable, profitable campaign
Your launch and kill rules are written down
You spend hours a day on repeatable tasks
You have cash for a few months of salary and test budget
You know what you would hand over first
steps.say: How do you know the timing is right? Hire too early and you burn cash and morale. Hire too late and you burn yourself out, with winning campaigns left unwatched. Look at the checklist. You have at least one stable, profitable campaign. Your launch and kill rules are written down. You spend hours a day on repeatable tasks. You have cash for a few months of salary and test budget. And you know exactly what you'd hand over first.

steps.p: A scorecard lists the outcomes the role must deliver and the traits that predict them. Write it before you post the job, then judge every candidate against it instead of against your mood in the interview.
steps.say: A scorecard lists the outcomes the role must deliver and the traits that predict them. Write it before you post the job. Look at the table. Numbers: can they calculate C P A, cost per acquisition, R O I and headroom fast? Test that with a short maths test. Discipline, with a paid test task. Honesty, through references and the trial. Compliance, with a copy review exercise. And learning, with a second round of the task. Then judge every candidate against this, not against your mood in the interview.

steps.p: The best buyers are often not people with buyer on their CV. Look for people who already show the habits: careful with numbers, curious and honest.
d: Your own community|students who did the work
Adjacent roles|analysts, sales ops, teachers of maths
Interns|trained from zero on your SOPs
steps.say: Where do good candidates come from? Often not from people with buyer on their C V. Look for the habits instead: careful with numbers, curious and honest. Check the cards. Your own community, students who actually did the work. Adjacent roles like analysts, sales ops, or maths teachers. Referrals from people you trust. Junior buyers with small accounts but good habits. And interns you train from zero on your S O Ps, your standard operating procedures.

steps.p: Each step filters for something different. Paying for the test task is fair and attracts serious people. Keep the whole process under three weeks so good candidates do not accept other offers.
steps.say: Here's a hiring process that works. Follow the flow: scorecard and post, a short screening call, a paid test task, a review together, a reference check, then a paid trial period. Each step filters for something different. Paying for the test task is fair, and it attracts serious people. And keep the whole process under three weeks, so good candidates don't accept other offers while you wait.

steps.h: Inviting a candidate to the test task
steps.p: Example message after the screening call. It states the pay, the time it should take, the deadline and what happens next, so serious candidates can plan and nobody works for free on a vague promise.

messages.text: Thanks for the call today. Next step is a paid test task: about 2 hours, paid $25, using anonymised campaign data.
Deadline is Friday 6pm. We review it together on Monday. Instructions and the rule card are attached.
Thank you. I will send it on Thursday evening.

steps.say: This is an example message after the screening call. Notice what it states clearly. The pay, twenty five dollars. The time, about two hours, using anonymised campaign data. The deadline, Friday at six p m, and the review on Monday. The instructions and rule card are attached. That way serious candidates can plan, and nobody works for free on a vague promise. And look, the candidate replies with when she'll send it.

steps.h: Walkthrough: score candidates on the sheet
steps.p: Score every candidate on the scorecard areas from 1 to 5, straight after each step, before you discuss them with anyone. The totals stop a confident talker from beating a careful worker. Example scores.
steps.more: Check the maths: Amaka 4 + 5 + 5 + 4 + 4 = 22. Musa 5 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 15. Musa was the most impressive talker in the interview; the sheet shows weak discipline and compliance, the two areas that cost the most later.
steps.say: Now score candidates on a sheet. Rate each one from one to five on every scorecard area, straight after each step, before you discuss them with anyone. These are example scores. Amaka totals twenty two. Musa totals fifteen. Efua totals twenty. Here's the interesting part. Musa was the most impressive talker in the interview, but the sheet shows weak discipline and compliance, the two areas that cost the most later. The totals stop a confident talker from beating a careful worker. Amaka moves to the paid trial.

steps.p: Example: give the candidate a spreadsheet of 14 days of real, anonymised campaign data. Ask them to mark which ad sets to kill, hold and scale using your written rule card, explain why, and write one compliant ad for the winning angle. Your rules should match the Budget and kill rules module.

d.text: You learn how they read numbers, how they explain decisions and whether they write honest copy, in about two hours of their time.

steps.say: Here's an example test task. Give the candidate a spreadsheet of fourteen days of real, anonymised campaign data. Ask them to mark which ad sets to kill, hold and scale using your written rule card, and explain why. Then ask for one compliant ad for the winning angle. Your rules should match the Budget and kill rules module. In about two hours of their time, you learn how they read numbers, how they explain decisions, and whether they write honest copy.

steps.p: Confidence is not competence. Some of the most expensive hires talk well about big results they cannot show. Listen for how candidates treat numbers and mistakes.

b.title: Good signs
items: Explains a loss and the lesson
Talks about policy without being asked

steps.say: In the interview, remember, confidence is not competence. Some of the most expensive hires talk well about big results they can't show. On the left, the warning signs: big R O A S claims with no records, blaming platforms for every loss, offering account tricks, and being vague about past spend. On the right, the good signs: they show sheets and logs, explain a loss and the lesson, talk about policy without being asked, and ask about your rules.

steps.p: Candidates who offer bought accounts, cloaking or 'ways around review' are telling you how they will treat your business. Do not hire them, however good their numbers sound.

d.text: One person using banned methods can get every asset in your business restricted.

steps.say: This one is a firm warning. Candidates who offer bought accounts, cloaking, or ways around review are telling you how they'll treat your business. Don't hire them, however good their numbers sound. Here's why it matters so much: one person using banned methods can get every asset in your business restricted.

steps.p: Agree these lines in writing on the first day of a paid trial, so the decision at the end is a check, not an argument. Example for a 30-day trial. Starting rules; adapt them to your team and offers.
steps.say: When the paid trial starts, agree these lines in writing on day one. Then the decision at the end is a check, not an argument. This is an example for a thirty day trial. Rule card followed on every ad set. Daily report on time every working day. Disapproval rate at or below the team average. Confirmed C P A falling week on week. And any banned method ends the trial that same day. These are starting rules, so adapt them to your team and offers.

steps.p: These mistakes are expensive because you pay for them for months. Each one on the left feels efficient at the time. The fixes on the right add a few days to hiring and save far more later.
steps.say: Now some common hiring mistakes. They're expensive because you pay for them for months, and each one feels efficient at the time. On the left: hiring before rules exist, hiring the best talker, unpaid test tasks, and no written trial goals. On the right, the fixes: write rules, then hire. Judge on the scorecard. Pay for the test. And agree trial goals in writing. These add a few days to hiring and save far more later.

steps.h: Worked example: cost of a new buyer
steps.p: Example: a new buyer costs $500 a month in salary and you set aside $1,500 of test budget over the first two months, which you expect to mostly lose while they learn. Total cost by the end of month two: $2,500.

d.label: cost of first two months
d.note: Example figures. Local pay varies widely.

steps.more: Check the maths: 2 × $500 salary + $1,500 test budget = $2,500. Now suppose that from month three the buyer produces $1,000 a month of net profit before their salary. After paying salary, that is $500 a month towards the $2,500. Payback takes five more months, so the hire breaks even around the end of month seven.
steps.say: Let's work out what a new buyer costs. This is an example. Salary is five hundred dollars a month, and you set aside one thousand five hundred dollars of test budget over the first two months, which you expect to mostly lose while they learn. Two months of salary plus the test budget gives two thousand five hundred dollars. Now suppose from month three they produce one thousand dollars a month of net profit before salary. After salary, that's five hundred a month back, so payback takes five more months. Local pay varies widely.

steps.p: Example from the last slide. Cumulative amount still to recover at the end of each month, from month two to month seven. Plan your cash for this whole period, not just the first salary.
steps.say: Here's that same example as payback by month. Each bar is the amount still to recover. Month two, two thousand five hundred dollars. Then it drops by five hundred each month: two thousand, one thousand five hundred, one thousand, five hundred, and zero at month seven. The lesson is in the shape. Plan your cash for this whole period, not just the first salary.

steps.p: Prepare these before the new buyer starts. A buyer who spends their first week waiting for logins and answers learns that your operation is disorganised, and that lesson is hard to undo.
d: Own login with the right role, 2FA on
steps.say: Before day one, prepare everything on this checklist. Contract and confidentiality signed. Their own login with the right role, and two factor authentication, two F A, switched on. The S O P folder shared. A training plan for thirty days. And a named person to answer questions. Why bother? A buyer who spends their first week waiting for logins learns that your operation is disorganised, and that lesson is hard to undo.

steps.p: Take time to hire well. If a trial does not work, end it kindly, quickly and on the terms agreed at the start. Keeping the wrong person costs more than starting again.

d.b: Clear terms make hard calls easier
d.s: Agree trial length and goals in writing

steps.say: To close, take your time to hire well. And if a trial doesn't work, end it kindly, quickly, and on the terms you agreed at the start. Clear terms make hard calls easier, so agree the trial length and goals in writing. Keeping the wrong person costs more than starting again.

takeaways: Hire to scale a proven system, with written rules already in place.
Use a scorecard, a paid test task and a paid trial to judge real ability.
Plan the cash for the full payback period, often several months.

glossary.def: A written list of the outcomes a role must deliver and how candidates will be tested on each.
A short, paid exercise using realistic work that shows how a candidate thinks and works.
An agreed paid period with clear goals, after which both sides decide whether to continue.
How long it takes for a hire's contribution to recover what they cost to hire and train.

quiz.q: When is the best time to hire your first buyer?
options: When you have a stable winner and written rules
Before you have any profitable campaign
As soon as you can afford one salary
quiz.why: A new buyer should scale a proven system. Without one, you cannot train or judge them fairly.

quiz.q: A buyer costs $600 a month. Test budget is $1,200 over two months. From month three they add $1,000 net profit a month before salary. When do they roughly break even?
quiz.why: Cost by month two: 2 × $600 + $1,200 = $2,400. Recovery after salary: $400 a month. $2,400 ÷ $400 = 6 more months, so the end of month 8.

quiz.q: A candidate offers to bring 'aged accounts that never get banned'. What do you do?
options: Hire them at a higher salary
Do not hire; they are offering banned methods
quiz.why: Someone selling banned methods puts every asset in your business at risk.

quiz.q: Why pay for the test task?
options: It is required by law everywhere
It is fair and attracts serious candidates
quiz.why: Paying respects the candidate's time and filters for people who take the work seriously.

quiz.q: Which interview answer is the strongest signal?
options: 'Here is a sheet of a loss and what I changed after'
'Platforms are unfair, that is why I lost'
'I know tricks to get past review'
quiz.why: Records and honest reflection on losses predict good performance.

lessons.title: Training buyers and delegating spend
objectives: By the end you can run a 30-day training plan for a new buyer.
By the end you can set spending authority levels with clear promotion rules.
By the end you can delegate decisions without losing control of risk.

steps.h: Training is how your rules survive you
steps.p: Every rule that lives only in your head is lost the day you are busy or away. Training turns your judgement into habits other people can repeat. The goal is a buyer who makes the decision you would make, without asking you.

d.b: Teach the why, not just the clicks

steps.say: Every rule that lives only in your head is lost the day you're busy or away. Training turns your judgement into habits other people can repeat. The goal is a buyer who makes the decision you would make, without asking you. And notice the subtitle: teach the why, not just the clicks. Buttons change. Principles last.

steps.p: Example plan. Each week adds responsibility only after the previous week's skills are shown in practice, not just understood in conversation. Slow buyers repeat a week; nobody skips one.
steps.more: Week one: the new buyer shadows a senior, fills the daily sheet and explains each decision back. Week two: they build campaigns from the SOP, but a senior approves before launch. Week three: they run a small sandbox budget on their own with fixed kill rules. Week four: you review their logs, disapproval rate and decisions together, then decide whether they move up a level.
steps.say: Here's an example thirty day ramp. Week one, watch and log: the new buyer shadows a senior, fills the daily sheet and explains each decision back. Week two, they build campaigns from the S O P, the standard operating procedure, but a senior approves before launch. Week three, they run a small sandbox budget on their own with fixed kill rules. Week four, you review their logs, disapproval rate and decisions together, then decide on the next level. Slow buyers repeat a week. Nobody skips one.

steps.p: Authority levels make delegation safe. Each level has a spend limit and rules. People move up by meeting written criteria, not by asking. Example limits only; set yours from your margins and cash.
steps.say: Authority levels make delegation safe. Each level has a spend limit and rules, and people move up by meeting written criteria, not by asking. Look at the table. A trainee gets fifty dollars per campaign and can do nothing without approval. A buyer gets three hundred dollars and can launch, kill and scale by the S O P. A senior gets one thousand five hundred and can approve trainee launches. A lead controls the team budget and sets rules. These are example limits only, so set yours from your margins and cash.

steps.h: Walkthrough: a hard limit for a trainee
steps.p: Back the authority table with a limit the platform enforces. Many ad platforms let you set an account spending limit; at the time of writing Meta has one in billing settings. We are not certain of current names, so check your Ads Manager.

blocks.value: Ads stop delivering when total spend reaches the limit. Reset or raise it only after a review.

steps.say: Back up that table with a limit the platform itself enforces. Many ad platforms let you set an account spending limit, and at the time of writing Meta has one in billing settings. We're not certain of the current names, so check your own Ads Manager. In this example, the training account has a limit of six hundred dollars. Ads stop delivering when total spend reaches the limit, and you reset or raise it only after a review.

steps.p: Write promotion criteria before anyone asks for a promotion. People work harder towards clear targets, and you avoid promotions that are really about who complains the most.
steps.say: Write promotion criteria before anyone asks for a promotion. People work harder towards clear targets, and you avoid promotions that are really about who complains the most. Here's an example list. Four weeks inside kill rules. Profitable on confirmed data. A disapproval rate below the team average. Reports on time every day. And they've passed the policy quiz.

steps.h: Worked example: risk at each level
steps.p: Example: a trainee runs three campaigns at the $50 daily limit, with a target CPA of $20. The zero-FTD kill line is 2 × $20 = $40. The most they can spend before every campaign with no FTD is stopped is $120.

d.label: most a trainee can lose with no FTDs

steps.more: Check the maths: 2 × $20 = $40 of spend with no FTD per campaign. Three campaigns × $40 = $120 before all are killed. You can afford that loss as training cost. Compare a trainee with no limit who leaves a $500 campaign running overnight. Authority levels limit the size of mistakes; they are not about trust. The kill lines come from the Budget and kill rules module.
steps.say: Let's see how levels limit risk. In this example, a trainee runs three campaigns at the fifty dollar daily limit, with a target C P A, cost per acquisition, of twenty dollars. The zero F T D kill line, F T D meaning first time deposit, is two times twenty, so forty dollars. Three campaigns times forty is one hundred and twenty dollars, the most they can lose before every campaign with no F T D is stopped. You can afford that as training cost. Authority levels limit the size of mistakes. They're not about trust.

steps.p: Delegating a task means telling someone what to do. Delegating an outcome means telling them what result you need and the limits, and letting them decide how. Senior people should get outcomes.

b.title: Outcome
items: Find one new winning angle this week

steps.say: There are two ways to delegate. Delegating a task means telling someone what to do. On the left: raise ad set four by twenty percent, launch these three ads. You decide each step. Delegating an outcome means telling them the result you need and the limits. On the right: keep C P A under twenty five dollars on four hundred a day, find one new winning angle this week, keep disapproval under ten percent. They decide inside the rules. Senior people should get outcomes.

steps.p: Most new buyers who fail were trained in a way that made failure likely. The mistakes on the left are common because they feel faster. The fixes on the right build buyers who decide the way you would.
steps.say: Most new buyers who fail were trained in a way that made failure likely. On the left, the common mistakes: teaching buttons before numbers, giving answers in reviews, feedback a month later, and promoting the loudest. On the right, the fixes: numbers, rules, policy, then tools. Questions that make them explain. Feedback within a day. And written promotion criteria. The mistakes feel faster, but the fixes build buyers who decide the way you would.

steps.p: Teach in this order. Each layer depends on the one before. A buyer who knows the buttons but not the numbers will scale losses with great confidence.
d: Policy|what never goes in an ad
steps.say: Teach in this order, because each layer depends on the one before. First numbers: C P A, headroom, and marginal C P A. Then rules: kill, hold, scale. Then policy: what never goes in an ad. Then tools: the platform, the tracker, the sheet. And finally judgement, reading unusual situations. Here's why the order matters. A buyer who knows the buttons but not the numbers will scale losses with great confidence.

steps.p: Example: a weekly review between a senior and a new buyer. The senior asks questions that make the buyer explain the reasoning, rather than giving the answer.

d.text: I killed ad set 2 on Tuesday. It spent $41 with no FTD.
Senior: Good, that passes the $40 line, 2 × our $20 target. What did the CTR and landing data say before you killed it?
CTR was fine but landing page views were low. I think the page loaded slowly on mobile.
Senior: Then test the page speed before you drop the angle. Log it as a page problem, not an angle problem.

steps.say: Here's an example weekly review between a senior and a new buyer. The buyer killed ad set two after it spent forty one dollars with no F T D. The senior confirms that passes the forty dollar line, then asks what the C T R, click through rate, and landing data said. The buyer notices landing page views were low, maybe a slow page on mobile. So the senior says test the page speed first, and log it as a page problem, not an angle problem. Notice the senior asks questions instead of giving the answer.

steps.p: Your trainee asks whether to kill an ad set. Apply the rule card yourself before you answer, then ask the trainee to explain their reasoning in the same order: zero-FTD kill, CPA kill, scale, then hold.

d.task: Target $20. A trainee's ad set: $41 spent in 3 days, 0 network-confirmed FTDs. Kill, hold or scale?

steps.say: Time for a lab. Your trainee asks whether to kill an ad set. The target is twenty dollars. The ad set has spent forty one dollars in three days, with zero network confirmed F T Ds. Should it be kill, hold or scale? Apply the rule card yourself first, then ask the trainee to explain their reasoning in the same order: zero F T D kill, C P A kill, scale, then hold. Pause and try it, then check your answer.

steps.p: Give feedback within a day of the decision, about the decision itself, with the numbers on screen. General comments a month later rarely change behaviour.

d.text: Praise good process even when the result lost money. Correct bad process even when the result made money.

steps.say: Feedback only sticks when it's quick and specific. Give it within a day of the decision, about the decision itself, with the numbers on screen. General comments a month later rarely change behaviour. And here's the key tip: praise good process even when the result lost money, and correct bad process even when the result made money.

steps.p: Illustration: a new buyer's confirmed CPA per week against a $25 target during the first seven weeks. Expect costs above target at first. What matters is the direction and whether the same mistakes repeat.
steps.say: This chart is an illustration of a typical learning curve. The falling line is a new buyer's confirmed C P A each week. The flat line is the twenty five dollar target. Week one starts at forty eight dollars, then it drops steadily, reaching twenty five in week six and twenty three in week seven. So expect costs above target at first. What matters is the direction, and whether the same mistakes repeat.

steps.p: Delegation works best when limits are automatic rather than remembered. Use these guardrails so that a single bad decision by anyone, including you, cannot grow into a large loss overnight.
d: Account spending limits set in the platform
Senior reviews any campaign over limit
steps.say: Delegation works best when limits are automatic rather than remembered. Use these guardrails. Spend limits by level. Account spending limits set in the platform. A daily report before noon. A senior reviews any campaign over limit. And all launches pass compliance review. Together they mean a single bad decision by anyone, including you, can't grow into a large loss overnight.

steps.p: Authority levels change how much someone may spend, never what they may say or where they may run. No level allows a buyer to skip compliance review, use claims outside the register or run a regulated offer in a geo without authorization.

d.text: Seniority is not an exemption. The founder's ads go through review too.

steps.say: This is important. Authority levels change how much someone may spend, never what they may say or where they may run. No level lets a buyer skip compliance review, use claims outside the register, or run a regulated offer in a geo without authorization. Seniority is not an exemption. The founder's ads go through review too.

steps.p: Once you delegate, your job is no longer to make every decision. It is to set the rules, check the system and coach the people. That is harder at first and the only way to grow beyond one person.

d.s: You run the system; the team runs the campaigns

steps.say: Finally, once you delegate, your job changes. It's no longer to make every decision. It's to set the rules, check the system, and coach the people. You go from buyer to builder. You run the system, and the team runs the campaigns. That's harder at first, and it's the only way to grow beyond one person.

lessons.title: SOPs and the tools stack
objectives: By the end you can write a standard operating procedure someone else can follow.
By the end you can list the core SOPs a media buying team needs.
By the end you can choose a lean tools stack and control who has access to it.

steps.h: An SOP is a decision you made once
steps.p: A standard operating procedure, or SOP, is a written set of steps for a task that happens again and again. Each one saves you from making the same decision every day and lets anyone on the team do the task the same way.

d.b: Write it once, run it a thousand times
d.s: SOPs turn your habits into the team's habits

steps.say: A standard operating procedure, or S O P, is a written set of steps for a task that happens again and again. Each one saves you from making the same decision every day, and lets anyone on the team do the task the same way. Write it once, run it a thousand times. S O Ps turn your habits into the team's habits.

steps.p: Keep the same structure for every SOP so people know where to look. Short is better. If an SOP is longer than one or two pages, it is probably two SOPs.

rows: What must be true before done

steps.say: Every S O P should have the same structure, so people know where to look. Look at the table. A title, like launch a new campaign. An owner, like the senior buyer. A trigger, like a new angle approved. Numbered steps, one action each. Checks, meaning what must be true before it's done. And a version and date. Keep it short. If an S O P runs longer than one or two pages, it's probably two S O Ps.

steps.h: Core SOPs for a buying team
steps.p: Start with the tasks that cost the most when they are done wrong. Most buying teams need these six SOPs before anything else, and many never need more than ten.
steps.say: Start with the tasks that cost the most when they're done wrong. Most buying teams need these six first. Launch, covering structure, naming and a tracking check. Daily check, for spend, C P A, cost per acquisition, status and comments. Kill, hold, scale, the rules with numbers. Creative review, a policy and claims checklist. Access, for adding and removing people. And incident, for a restriction or a tracking failure. Many teams never need more than ten.

steps.p: A launch SOP makes every campaign start the same way, so results are comparable and nothing is forgotten. Platform names change; keep the SOP about principles and update the button names when needed.
steps.say: Here's an example launch S O P. Follow the flow: an approved brief and creative, a name by convention, tracking and events tested, budget within authority, compliance check passed, then launch and log. This makes every campaign start the same way, so results are comparable and nothing gets forgotten. Platform names change, so keep the S O P about principles and update the button names when needed.

steps.p: Example daily check for each buyer, done before noon. The answers go into the daily report, so the check and the report are one job, not two.
d: Spend versus plan for each campaign
CPA versus kill and scale rules
Comments answered or hidden if spam
Landing pages load on a phone
steps.say: Here's an example daily check, done by each buyer before noon. Spend versus plan for each campaign. C P A versus the kill and scale rules. Any rejected ads or restrictions. Comments answered, or hidden if they're spam. Landing pages loading on a phone. And the actions taken, and why. steps.p: This SOP is the rule card itself, written so every buyer applies it the same way. Check the rows from the top and stop at the first that is true. Starting rules; adapt them to your vertical and data. Full rules: Budget and kill rules module.

3+ conversions, CPA ≤ 0.8 × target, 48 h+ since last step

steps.say: This S O P is the rule card itself, using network confirmed numbers only. Check the rows from the top and stop at the first that's true. lessons.title: Reporting that drives decisions
objectives: By the end you can set a daily, weekly and monthly reporting rhythm.
By the end you can build a weekly report that uses confirmed numbers.
By the end you can run a short meeting that ends in decisions, not just updates.

steps.p: A report that nobody acts on is a waste of the time it took to write. Every report should answer one question: what are we going to do differently because of these numbers?
steps.say: A report that nobody acts on is a waste of the time it took to write. So every report should answer one question: what are we going to do differently because of these numbers? No decision, no report. Numbers in, actions out.

steps.p: Different decisions need different time frames. Daily is for safety, weekly is for direction and monthly is for money. This is an example rhythm; adjust it to your team.

rows: Is anything broken or over limit?
What do we scale, fix or stop?
Did we make money after everything?

steps.say: Different decisions need different time frames. Look at the table. Daily, before noon, the question is: is anything broken or over limit? Weekly, on Friday: what do we scale, fix or stop? Monthly, in the first week: did we make money after everything? So daily is for safety, weekly is for direction, and monthly is for money. This is an example rhythm, so adjust it to your team.

steps.p: Example: a buyer's daily message in the team channel. It is short, puts confirmed numbers first, states the actions taken and flags problems without drama, so a lead can read it in a minute. Platform numbers appear only for comparison.

d.text: Daily, 3 Oct. Spend $612 of $650 plan. Network FTDs so far 22, CPA $27.82 (platform shows 26).
Killed 2 ad sets at the zero-FTD line. Stepped NG_PROOF by 20%. One ad rejected for claims; edited from the register and resubmitted.
Flag: landing page slow on mobile since 9pm. Asked dev to check.

steps.say: Here's an example daily update in the team channel. Spend six hundred and twelve dollars of a six hundred and fifty plan. Twenty two network F T Ds, first time deposits, and a C P A, cost per acquisition, of about twenty seven dollars eighty, with the platform figure shown only for comparison. Then actions: two ad sets killed at the zero F T D line, one stepped up by twenty percent, one rejected ad fixed and resubmitted. And a calm flag about a slow landing page. A lead can read it in a minute.

steps.p: Give every buyer the same template so updates can be read side by side. Confirmed numbers come first, then actions with the rule that triggered them, then flags. Keep it under one screen.

Confirmed numbers first: spend against plan, network F T Ds and C P A, with the platform number beside it. Then the actions taken, with the rule that triggered them. Then rejections, and flags. Keep it under one screen. And note this: no names, phone numbers or chats of leads in reports.

steps.p: Example weekly numbers for one buyer. Note the gap between platform-reported and network-confirmed results. All scaling and budget decisions use the confirmed column, never the platform one.
steps.more: Check the maths. Platform: $4,200 ÷ 168 = $25. Confirmed: $4,200 ÷ 140 = $30. Revenue: 140 × $40 = $5,600. Profit: $5,600 − $4,200 = $1,400. ROI: $1,400 ÷ $4,200 = 33.3%. On platform numbers the week looks almost twice as good as it was. A team that reports platform numbers will over-scale.
steps.say: Here's an example weekly report for one buyer, with two columns: platform and confirmed. Spend is four thousand two hundred dollars in both. The platform shows one hundred and sixty eight F T Ds, at a twenty five dollar C P A. The network confirmed one hundred and forty, at thirty dollars. At a forty dollar payout, confirmed profit is one thousand four hundred dollars, an R O I of about thirty three percent, against sixty percent on platform numbers. So the week looks almost twice as good as it was. Make every decision on the confirmed column, or you'll over scale.

steps.p: Example from the last slide: the network confirmed 140 of 168 platform FTDs, about 83%. Track this match rate weekly. A sudden drop means a tracking problem or a traffic quality problem.
steps.say: From that example, the network confirmed one hundred and forty of one hundred and sixty eight platform F T Ds. That's about eighty three percent, and it's called the match rate. Track it every week. A sudden drop means either a tracking problem or a traffic quality problem.

steps.p: Keep the same layout every week so trends are easy to see at a glance. Use one page per buyer and one summary page for the whole team.
d: Spend, confirmed FTDs, CPA, profit, ROI

Budget steps and marginal C P A. Tests launched and their results. Creatives near fatigue. And rejections and compliance notes. Use one page per buyer, and one summary page for the whole team.

steps.p: The lead reads one summary page before the weekly meeting. One row per buyer, confirmed numbers only, with the match rate beside them. Anything outside the rules is flagged before the meeting starts. Example figures, payout $40.

steps.p: Some numbers in a report should trigger an action automatically, without waiting for the meeting. Example lines; they are starting rules, so adapt them to your team and offers and write them in the reporting SOP.

rows: Match rate down 10+ points in a week
Buyer CPA above break-even for the week
Kill rules review with the lead

steps.say: Some numbers should trigger an action straight away, without waiting for the meeting. If the match rate drops ten or more points in a week, check tracking before any budget step. If a buyer's C P A is above break even for the week, review the kill rules with the lead. If a daily update is missing by noon, the lead checks that buyer's accounts. And if spend runs twenty percent or more over plan, it's explained in the same update. These are example starting rules, so adapt them and write them into your reporting S O P.

steps.p: Read the reports before the meeting, not in it. Use the time for decisions. End with a written list of who does what by when.
steps.say: Here's a thirty minute weekly meeting. Reports are read in advance, not in the meeting. Then ten minutes on wins and losses, ten minutes on problems and causes, and ten minutes on decisions and owners. Finally, the actions are written and shared. The point is to end with a written list of who does what by when.

steps.p: Two meetings look at exactly the same numbers. One produces information and everyone leaves feeling busy. The other produces action, and next week's problems are smaller.
steps.say: Two meetings can look at exactly the same numbers. On the left, the update meeting: everyone reads their numbers aloud, nobody challenges anything, it ends with keep going, and the same problems come back next week. On the right, the decision meeting: numbers read before, questions about causes, it ends with owners and dates, and problems close week by week. One produces information. The other produces action.

steps.p: Once a month, look at the whole business, not just campaigns. This is where you see whether growth is real after every cost and every network adjustment.
d: Plan|budgets and hires for next month
steps.say: Once a month, look at the whole business, not just campaigns. Check payouts received against confirmed earnings. All costs: spend, salaries, tools and creative. Net profit, after everything. Your cash position and next month's needs. And the plan, budgets and hires for next month. This is where you see whether growth is real after every cost and every network adjustment.

d.b: Same numbers, same format, every week

lessons.title: Creative pipeline and incentives
objectives: By the end you can run a creative production pipeline that meets your spend's demand.
By the end you can design buyer incentives based on confirmed net profit.
By the end you can spot incentive designs that reward the wrong behaviour.

steps.h: Creative is the engine of scale
steps.p: At scale, creative supply often limits growth before budget does. A pipeline turns creative from a burst of inspiration into a steady flow you can plan, measure and improve each week.

d.b: Steady flow beats bursts of genius
d.s: Plan creative like you plan budget

steps.say: At scale, creative supply often limits growth before budget does. A pipeline turns creative from a burst of inspiration into a steady flow you can plan, measure and improve every week. Steady flow beats bursts of genius. Plan creative like you plan budget.

steps.p: Every creative moves through the same stages. Each stage has an owner and a deadline. Learnings from the last stage feed the first, so the pipeline gets smarter every week.
steps.say: Every creative moves through the same stages. Follow the flow: idea and angle, brief, produce, compliance review, launch test, and learn and log. Each stage has an owner and a deadline. And look at the end: the learnings from the last stage feed back into the first, so the pipeline gets smarter every week.

steps.p: Example: from 40 raw ideas, 20 become briefs, 15 get produced, 12 pass compliance review and 2 become winners. That is a 2 in 15 hit rate on produced creatives.
steps.more: Use the funnel to plan. If you need 3 winners a week instead of 2, and every stage keeps its rate, you need about 50% more at every stage: 60 ideas, 30 briefs, about 23 produced. Or improve a rate: better briefs might lift the winner rate, which is cheaper than producing more. Track which stage loses the most and fix that one first.
steps.say: Here's an example weekly creative funnel. From forty raw ideas, twenty become briefs, fifteen get produced, twelve pass compliance review, and two become winners. That's two winners from fifteen produced. Now use it to plan. If you need three winners a week, and every rate stays the same, you need about fifty percent more at every stage. Or improve a rate instead, like better briefs, which is cheaper than producing more. Track which stage loses the most and fix that one first.

steps.p: Here is a different week. Work out the pass-through rate of each stage, the share that moves on to the next stage, and pick the lowest. That stage is where a fix pays back most, before you produce more of anything.

steps.p: One sheet sets the quota from spend and logs every angle. The example rule from the Scaling mechanics module is one new creative a week for each $100 of daily spend. Adjust it from your own hit rate. Example figures.

steps.p: A brief is how a buyer tells a creator exactly what to make. A clear brief saves rounds of edits and keeps claims inside the rules.

Winners and losers logged with reasons

steps.p: Each new creative is judged with the same rule card as any ad set. Example: target $30, break-even $40. Starting rules; adapt them to your vertical and data. Full method: Creative testing lab module.

steps.say: Each new creative is judged with the same rule card as any ad set, on network confirmed results. In this example the target is thirty dollars and break even is forty. Zero F T Ds, first time deposits, at sixty dollars spent: kill and log the reason. Ninety dollars or more spent with C P A over forty: kill. Three or more F T Ds with C P A at or below twenty four: a winner, so move it to scaling. C T R thirty percent or more below its best with rising frequency: fatigue, so replace it. Anything else, hold. Adapt these starting rules.

steps.p: Once a brief and angle are approved, more variations of the same idea raise your chance of a winner without new research. Every variation still passes the same review as a hand-made ad.

steps.h: You get what you pay for
steps.p: Incentives tell people what you really value, louder than any speech. Pay buyers on spend and they will spend. Pay them on platform revenue and they will chase cheap, low-quality results. Pay them on confirmed net profit inside the rules.

d.b: Pay for confirmed profit, inside the rules

steps.say: Now incentives. They tell people what you really value, louder than any speech. Pay buyers on spend, and they'll spend. Pay them on platform revenue, and they'll chase cheap, low quality results. So pay them on confirmed net profit, inside the rules. Incentives are instructions people follow.

steps.p: Each bad design here has been tried by many operators, and each one produced exactly the behaviour it rewarded. Compare what each column would make a buyer do on a slow week.

And no link to compliance. On the right: a percent of confirmed net profit, after all direct costs, with part held back for reversals, and a compliance breach that cancels the bonus. Ask yourself what each column would make a buyer do on a slow week.

steps.h: The five parts of a pay plan
steps.p: Every pay plan in this lesson has the same five parts. Write each one down and give it to the person before the period starts. If a part is missing, that is where the payday argument will come from.
d: Base pay|steady income for learning and admin
Gates|rules that cancel or cut a bonus
Review date|when the plan can change
steps.say: Every pay plan here has the same five parts. Base pay, for steady income while learning and doing admin. A bonus, as a share of confirmed net profit. A holdback, the part paid after payouts arrive. Gates, the rules that cancel or cut a bonus. And a review date, for when the plan can change. Write each one down and give it to the person before the period starts. If a part is missing, that's where the payday argument will come from.

steps.p: Example mix by level. Trainees get base pay only, because their sandbox results are mostly luck and learning. Profit share grows with authority. Percentages are illustrative; set yours from your margins, and local pay varies widely.

steps.say: Here's an example mix by level. Trainees get base pay only, because their sandbox results are mostly luck and learning. A buyer gets base plus eight percent of their own net profit. A senior gets base, ten percent of their own net, and a small team share. A lead gets base plus a share of team net profit. So profit share grows with authority. These percentages are illustrative, so set yours from your margins.

steps.p: A holdback must cover the bonus you would claw back if the network reverses some FTDs. Use your own reversal rate from the last three months, not a guess. The formula gives the share of the bonus to hold.
steps.more: Why it works: a reversal removes revenue, so net profit and the bonus fall by the same share of revenue. Holding back that share of the bonus means reversals come out of money you have not paid yet.
steps.say: A holdback must cover the bonus you'd claw back if the network reverses some F T Ds. The formula on screen: reversal rate, times revenue divided by net profit, equals the holdback share. Use your own reversal rate from the last three months, not a guess. Why does it work? A reversal removes revenue, so net profit and the bonus fall by the same share of revenue. Holding back that share means reversals come out of money you haven't paid yet.

steps.h: Worked example: how much to hold
steps.p: Example using the bonus from the last lesson: revenue $30,000, net profit $7,000, bonus 10%. With a 5% reversal rate the holdback should be about 21% of the bonus. With 10% reversals it needs about 43%.
steps.more: Check the maths: 5% of $30,000 = $1,500 reversed. Bonus falls by 10% × $1,500 = $150. $150 ÷ $700 = 21.4%. At 10%: $3,000 reversed, bonus falls by $300, $300 ÷ $700 = 42.9%. This is why the last lesson's 20% holdback left you $160 overpaid after $3,000 of reversals.
steps.say: Let's work an example, using last lesson's numbers: revenue thirty thousand dollars, net profit seven thousand, bonus ten percent, so seven hundred dollars. At a five percent reversal rate, one thousand five hundred of revenue is reversed, and the bonus falls by one hundred and fifty, about twenty one percent of the bonus. At ten percent reversals, three thousand is reversed and the bonus falls by three hundred, about forty three percent. That's why last lesson's twenty percent holdback left you overpaid.

steps.h: Gates that cancel or cut a bonus
steps.p: Gates make the rules part of the pay. Agree them in writing before the period starts and apply them to everyone the same way, including seniors. Starting rules; a lawyer should check how they fit your contracts.

rows: Serious policy breach, e.g. cloaking, false claims
Bonus cut by the agreed amount

steps.say: Gates make the rules part of the pay. A serious policy breach, for example cloaking or false claims, cancels the bonus for the period. A kill rule ignored on purpose cuts the bonus by the agreed amount. F T Ds reversed by the network are recalculated from the holdback. And rules changed mid month apply next period only. Agree these in writing and apply them to everyone, including seniors. These are starting rules, and a lawyer should check how they fit your contracts.

steps.p: Many networks pay some weeks after month end, with terms that vary. Pay the confirmed part on payday and the holdback after the money arrives, so you never pay bonuses from cash you have not received. Check your own network terms.
steps.say: Many networks pay some weeks after month end, and the terms vary, so check your own. Follow the flow: the month ends, net profit is worked out on confirmed data, the paid now part goes out on payday, the network payout arrives, and then the holdback is recalculated and paid. That way you never pay bonuses from cash you haven't received.

steps.p: Pay mistakes cost twice: once in money and again in trust. Each mistake on the left has a fix on the right that costs nothing but a written page agreed in advance.
steps.say: Pay mistakes cost twice, once in money and again in trust. On the right, the fixes: a percent of confirmed net profit, changes that start next period, a holdback until payout arrives, and proper contracts and pay records. Each fix costs nothing but a written page agreed in advance.
